emergencyNumber: 112 (EU emergency — ambulance, fire, police), 110 (police only), 116 117 (medical on-call service / ärztlicher Bereitschaftsdienst)
healthcareSystem: Universal (Gesetzliche Krankenversicherung / GKV — statutory health insurance, mandatory for residents)
qualityNotes: One of the best healthcare systems in the world. Highly trained doctors, excellent hospitals. English is commonly spoken in medical settings in major cities. Wait times are generally short. Everyone pays for health insurance — even tourists should have coverage.
pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 8:30am-6:30pm weekdays, 9am-4pm Saturdays. Some pharmacies in major cities have late-night hours. An 'Apothekennotdienst' (emergency pharmacy) is always available nearby — check online or ask any pharmacy for the nearest on-duty pharmacy.
pharmacyTips: Pharmacies (Apotheke) are widely available. Most medications require a prescription. Pharmacists are highly trained and can advise on minor ailments. Look for the red 'A' sign.
prescriptionRules: EU prescriptions are accepted. Non-EU prescriptions require a German doctor's verification. Germany has strict prescription rules — many antibiotics and medications require a prescription.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine products require a prescription in Germany. Small quantities may be available with pharmacist consultation.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, methylphenidate)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances requiring a German prescription or special import permit from the Bundesinstitut für Arzneimittel (BfArM). Some ADHD medications are not available in Germany.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines (Valium/diazepam, Xanax/alprazolam)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. A valid prescription is required. Germany has strict rules around benzodiazepine prescriptions.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Medical cannabis is legal for specific conditions but requires a prescription from a German doctor. Tourists cannot bring cannabis products into Germany.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter and prescription (ideally in German or English) for all medications. Bring sufficient supply in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry prescription documentation at all times. EU citizens should carry the EHIC card.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not legally required for short stays, but strongly recommended. EU citizens should carry EHIC/GHIC.
travelInsurance.tips: Hospitals will treat emergencies without payment upfront in most cases, but you may be billed later. Travel insurance with comprehensive medical coverage and 24/7 assistance is essential. German hospitals are excellent but costs can be high without insurance.

recommended: Hepatitis A (for close contact with locals)
Tick-borne encephalitis (FSME — for rural areas, especially southern Germany)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers. FSME vaccination is recommended if visiting rural/forested areas in spring/summer.

waterNotes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Germany. Germany has some of the best drinking water quality in the world.
foodSafetyTips: Excellent food safety standards. German cuisine is hearty — be aware of rich foods, pork, and sauerkraut if your stomach isn't used to them. Raw minced meat (Mett) is popular — it's safe from reputable sources. Cheese and dairy are generally safe. Watch out for pork-heavy dishes.
medicalTourismNote: Germany is a top destination for medical tourism, particularly for cancer treatment, cardiovascular procedures, and orthopedics. High quality, moderate costs compared to the US.
sources: Germany Federal Ministry of Health (Bundesministerium für Gesundheit)
metaDescription: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Germany. Emergency numbers (112, 110), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, vaccination requirements, and travel insurance advice.
